mcqs.question: A cookie is set with SameSite=Lax. A user clicks a link on an external site that navigates to your app, and separately, an external site embeds an tag pointing at your API. What happens to the cookie in each case?
options: The cookie is sent in neither case, since Lax blocks all cross-site requests
The cookie is sent in both cases identically, since Lax only distinguishes HTTP from HTTPS
The cookie is sent on the top-level link-click navigation, but not on the cross-site image request
The cookie is sent on the image request but not the link click, since images are always considered same-site
mcqs.explanation: Lax allows cookies on top-level navigations like clicking a link, but withholds them on subresource requests triggered from another site, such as an embedded image or a background fetch. That asymmetry is exactly why Lax mitigates a large class of CSRF without breaking normal link-based navigation.

mcqs.question: An app stores a 2MB JSON blob in localStorage and reads it on every route change. What's the concrete performance concern?
options: localStorage automatically compresses data, adding CPU overhead on every read
localStorage reads and writes are synchronous and block the main thread, so a large read on every navigation adds real, measurable jank
localStorage silently caps individual reads at 1MB, truncating the returned data
localStorage requires a network round trip to the origin server on every access
mcqs.explanation: Unlike IndexedDB's async API, localStorage's get/set calls run synchronously on the main thread, so a large read blocks everything else — script execution, layout, input handling — for however long that read takes.

mcqs.question: Which storage mechanism is the only one automatically attached to outgoing requests, with no JavaScript needing to run at all?
options: sessionStorage
IndexedDB
localStorage
Cookies
mcqs.explanation: Cookies are the one mechanism the browser itself attaches to matching requests. The other three are inert data at rest — a server only sees their contents if your JavaScript explicitly reads them and sends the value.

mcqs.question: Why can't document.cookie be used to read a cookie set with the HttpOnly flag?
options: HttpOnly cookies are deliberately hidden from JavaScript entirely — that's the specific defense the flag provides against theft via XSS
document.cookie can only read cookies that were set within the last hour
HttpOnly cookies are stored in a separate, JavaScript-inaccessible browser profile
document.cookie requires the Secure flag to be present on a cookie before it can read it
mcqs.explanation: HttpOnly exists specifically to make a cookie invisible to any JavaScript running on the page, including a malicious script injected via XSS — that's the entire point of the flag, not an incidental side effect.

mcqs.question: Why does storing an auth token in an HttpOnly cookie defend against XSS-based theft better than storing it in localStorage, even though both remain vulnerable to some attack?
options: HttpOnly cookies are encrypted at rest on disk, unlike localStorage values
localStorage is readable by any JavaScript on the page, including an injected XSS payload, while an HttpOnly cookie can't be read by JS at all, even from a successful XSS
HttpOnly cookies automatically expire after every page load, limiting the exposure window
localStorage values are shared across all origins by default, widening the attack surface
mcqs.explanation: The distinguishing property is readability, not encryption or expiry: localStorage hands the token to any script that runs on the page, XSS included, while HttpOnly removes JS read access entirely — the token stays invisible even when XSS succeeds. HttpOnly cookies still face CSRF, just not this specific theft vector.
